title: Agentic commerce adoption depends on payment-level control, reversibility, data visibility, and recognizable recourse rather than convenience alone
source_unit: Visa, Earning Consumer Trust in the Age of Agentic Commerce, based on Visa Agentic Commerce Consumer Research Surveys in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand
geography: United States, Australia, and New Zealand online shoppers; report page updated for Visa Intelligent Commerce and survey fieldwork identified as 2025

observations.period: 2025 survey fieldwork; U.S., Australia, and New Zealand familiarity and adoption frame

denominator.unit: online-shopping adults aged 18-65 with a debit or credit card: U.S. n=1600, Australia n=1600, New Zealand n=500

us_familiarity.unit: percent of U.S. respondents familiar with AI shopping assistants

australia_familiarity.unit: percent of Australian respondents familiar with AI shopping assistants

new_zealand_familiarity.unit: percent of New Zealand respondents familiar with AI shopping assistants

agent_consideration.value: 35% of U.S., 44% of Australian, and 34% of New Zealand respondents said an agent would increase consideration

adoption_route.value: consumers are pragmatic about AI shopping: savings, time, convenience, and comparison drive interest, while control and transparency condition adoption

observations.method: 15-minute online survey via AYTM among monthly online shoppers aged 18-65 holding a debit or credit card; national samples are described by Visa as representative online surveys, with respondents shown AI-assisted commerce scenarios across gifts, groceries, travel, and electronics.
observations.uncertainty: The report is Visa-sponsored, survey fieldwork is identified as 2025 despite the current report page, scenario responses are not observed transactions, and national representativeness does not establish causal adoption or payment outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Online shoppers in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand, with market-specific familiarity, motivators, and barriers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Familiarity and stated consideration may reflect scenario salience or brand framing; actual adoption may depend on merchant coverage, interface quality, regulation, and payment protections.

observations.period: 2025 survey fieldwork; agent substitution across the buyer journey

denominator.unit: online-shopping adults in the three-market Visa survey

discovery_substitution.unit: percent average substitution rate for discovery tasks across markets and use cases

evaluation_substitution.unit: percent average substitution rate for evaluation tasks

cart_checkout_substitution.unit: percent average substitution rate for cart and checkout tasks

post_purchase_substitution.unit: percent average substitution rate for tracking, returns, and warranty tasks

journey_route.value: agentic substitution spans discovery through post-purchase, making payment, returns, warranty, and recourse part of the trust surface

observations.method: Scenario-based survey estimates of tasks respondents might offload to AI assistants across four buyer-journey stages; rates are weighted averages across the three markets and use cases.
observations.uncertainty: Substitution rates represent stated willingness or scenario responses, not deployed-agent logs, completed purchases, return outcomes, fraud rates, or verified time savings.
observations.subgroup: Online shoppers across U.S., Australian, and New Zealand markets and four everyday shopping use cases.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may interpret “substitution” as assistance rather than full delegation; high discovery substitution can coexist with human approval at checkout and post-purchase.

observations.period: 2025 survey fieldwork; privacy, control, and error concerns

denominator.unit: online-shopping adults in the three-market Visa survey

data_control_important.unit: percent saying visibility into data collection and ability to customize or delete shopping and purchase information is important among U.S. respondents

stop_without_control.unit: percent saying they were not very or not at all likely to use an agent without control over data

wrong_product_concern.unit: percent average across markets concerned an agent could select the wrong product

loss_of_control_concern.unit: percent average across markets concerned about decisions being made without them

payment_recourse_route.value: transparency, fraud protection, refund policies, recognizable payment providers, and reversibility become part of the consumer control contract

observations.method: Survey questions on data visibility, customization and deletion, purchase accuracy, loss of control, reliability, privacy, and security; cross-market averages are reported separately from U.S.-specific data-control results.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not test actual deletion, refund, fraud, dispute, or reversal performance; reported preferences may vary by product risk, transaction size, agent design, and institutional safeguards.
observations.subgroup: Online shoppers in the U.S., Australia, and New Zealand, with U.S.-specific data-control results and cross-market concern averages.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consumers may accept limited data visibility when benefits are large, and recognizable payment brands can create trust without guaranteeing fair recourse or reliable agent behavior.

observations.period: 2025 survey fieldwork; human control and payment-infrastructure implications

denominator.unit: online-shopping adults in the three-market Visa survey

adoption_drivers.value: saving time, saving money, reducing repetitive work, better deals, and reducing decision fatigue

trust_requirements.value: nearly nine in ten want transparency into how agents make decisions, and about half would stop using them if control disappeared

human_ai_hybrid.value: hybrid experiences pairing human support with AI efficiency are proposed as a route to confidence in early-adoption markets

infrastructure_route.value: agentic commerce requires payment networks, issuers, acquirers, wallets, merchants, and developers to coordinate standards, identity, authentication, and consumer controls

observations.method: Visa interpretation of its multi-market survey findings and proposed payment-ecosystem implications; recommendations are strategic and sponsor-authored.
observations.uncertainty: The report's proposed infrastructure role for Visa is not an independent evaluation of standards, market power, consumer outcomes, or payment-sector competition.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, merchants, issuers, acquirers, wallets, developers, AI platforms, payment networks, and users needing human support or recourse.
observations.counterinterpretation: Interoperable agentic-payment infrastructure could improve security and convenience, but concentration in recognizable payment brands may also limit choice or shift control toward infrastructure intermediaries.

related_sources.claim: Official Visa report page with methodology, cross-market findings, data-control, substitution, and payment-infrastructure discussion.
Official 35-page Visa report PDF with appendix tables and market results.

boundary: This record adds a payment-control route from AI shopping assistance through discovery, evaluation, checkout, returns, data visibility, fraud protection, refunds, reversibility, and recognizable recourse. It uses a Visa-sponsored scenario survey whose fieldwork is identified as 2025, not observed transaction data, independent payment-infrastructure evaluation, causal adoption evidence, or proof that reported control preferences become durable safeguards.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Visa report page and PDF reviewed for market samples, survey frame, buyer-journey substitution rates, data-control findings, privacy and loss-of-control concerns, refund/reversibility language, and payment-ecosystem recommendations.
